answer:
I'd like to talk about a time when I completely changed my mind about learning to drive.

When I was eighteen, most of my friends were taking driving lessons, but I was firmly against it. I lived in a city with good public transport, so I thought a car would be an unnecessary expense. I also believed that driving was bad for the environment, and to be honest, I was a little nervous about being responsible for such a powerful machine.

What changed my mind was a summer job I took a couple of years later. I worked for a small charity that delivered food to elderly people living in villages outside the city. On the first day, my manager asked whether I could drive, and when I said no, I could see she was disappointed. For the whole summer, I had to rely on colleagues to take me everywhere, and I realised that in rural areas, a car isn't a luxury – it's often the only way to get around.

My manager was a big influence, too. She told me that being able to drive gives you independence and the ability to help others in an emergency. That really stuck with me.

So, that autumn, I signed up for lessons and passed my test on the second attempt. Afterwards, I felt a mixture of pride and relief. I still use public transport most of the time, but I'm glad I kept an open mind, because now I have the freedom to choose.

The skill I'd like to describe is video editing, which I taught myself online about two years ago.

At the time, I was helping to run a small hiking club, and we wanted to make short videos of our trips to attract new members. Nobody in the group knew how to edit, so I volunteered to learn. I downloaded a free editing program and started watching tutorials on a video-sharing website. There was one tutor in particular whose lessons were really clear – each video was only about ten minutes long and focused on one technique, like cutting clips, adding music or adjusting colours.

I practised almost every evening for about a month. To be honest, it was harder than I expected. The program had dozens of buttons and menus, and at first I kept losing my work because I forgot to save it. Getting the timing of music and images right was also tricky. Now I'd say I'm reasonably good at it. I've made around fifteen videos for the club, and our membership has nearly doubled. answer:
I'm going to talk about a very crowded place I visited: the main railway station in a large Asian city during a national holiday.

It was about three years ago, at the start of a long holiday weekend. I was travelling with a friend to visit her family in a town a few hours away. We'd been warned that the station would be busy, but nothing could have prepared us for what we saw.

The reason it was so crowded was that almost everyone in the city seemed to be leaving at the same time to visit relatives. There were thousands of people – families with huge suitcases, students carrying boxes of gifts, elderly people being helped along by their grandchildren. The queues for the ticket machines stretched right across the hall, and staff with loudspeakers were trying to guide people to the correct platforms. On the platform itself, people were standing shoulder to shoulder, and when the train arrived, it filled up in seconds.

At first, I felt quite anxious. I was worried about losing my friend, and it was very hot and noisy. But after a while, I started to find it fascinating. Even though it was so crowded, people were surprisingly patient and polite, and the system worked remarkably well – our train left exactly on time.

Looking back, I'm glad I experienced it, because it showed me how important family is in that culture. That said, next time I'll definitely try to travel on a quieter day!

answer:
The piece of advice I want to talk about came from my first manager, a woman called Mrs Adebayo, who ran the accounts department where I started my career.

It was during my first month there, and frankly, I was overwhelmed. I'd been given a project that was beyond my experience, and rather than asking for help, I'd been working late every night trying to work everything out on my own. One evening, she noticed I was still at my desk and asked how things were going. I admitted I was struggling, and she said something I've never forgotten: "Never spend more than an hour stuck on a problem without asking someone. Your time is valuable, and so is your sanity."

At first, I was a bit surprised, because I'd always assumed that asking questions would make me look incompetent. But she explained that in a team, the quickest way to solve most problems is to draw on other people's knowledge, and that experienced colleagues are usually happy to help if you ask early rather than at the last minute.

I think the advice was useful for several reasons. Practically, it saved me an enormous amount of time – what had taken me a whole day to figure out alone could often be solved in a ten-minute conversation. But it also changed my attitude. I stopped seeing asking for help as a weakness and started seeing it as part of working effectively. Since then, I've passed the same advice on to new colleagues, and I'm convinced it's one of the most valuable lessons I've learned.

I'd like to describe an old castle that I visited a few years ago, on a hill overlooking a small town in the south of my country.

It was built, as far as I remember, about five hundred years ago by a local lord. From the outside, it looks very impressive. It has thick grey stone walls, four round towers at the corners, and a narrow wooden bridge that leads over a dry moat to the main gate. Inside, there's a large courtyard, and several of the rooms have been restored with original furniture, tapestries and weapons.

I went there with my family, and we joined a guided tour, which was really informative. The guide explained that the castle was originally built to defend the town from attacks, and that it was besieged at least twice. Later, when the region became more peaceful, the family who owned it turned it into a luxurious home and added large windows and a beautiful garden. In the twentieth century, it was used as a school for a while, and then it was eventually bought by the government and turned into a museum.

What I remember most is how I felt when I climbed to the top of one of the towers. The view over the town and the river was spectacular, and I tried to imagine soldiers standing in the same spot, watching for enemies centuries ago. It made history feel much more real than reading about it in a textbook. I felt quite moved, actually, and it made me want to learn more about my own region's past.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
The invention I'd like to talk about is the washing machine. It might not sound very exciting compared with smartphones or the internet, but I think it has had a huge impact on everyday life.

Basically, a washing machine is a large drum that rotates while water and detergent are added. You put your dirty clothes inside, choose a programme depending on the type of fabric and temperature, and press start. The machine fills with water, washes the clothes by turning them over and over, rinses them, and then spins them at high speed to remove most of the water. Many modern machines can also dry clothes.

Before washing machines were common, washing clothes was an extremely time-consuming and physically demanding job. My grandmother told me that when she was young, she spent almost an entire day each week washing her family's clothes by hand, using a washboard and boiling water. Most of this work was done by women, so the washing machine freed up a great deal of their time. Some historians even argue that it helped more women to go out to work and continue their education.

Personally, I think the change has been overwhelmingly positive. It has saved billions of hours of hard labour and improved hygiene. Of course, washing machines do use a lot of electricity and water, so there is an environmental cost, but newer models are much more efficient than older ones. Overall, I'd say it's one of the most underrated inventions in history.

I'm going to talk about a time when I had to wait for my exam results after I finished high school.

At the end of my last year of school, I took the national university entrance exams. These exams were very important, because the results decided which university I could go to. After the exams finished in June, we had to wait about six weeks for the results to come out.

During those six weeks, I tried to keep busy. I got a part-time job in a café near my house, so I worked there four days a week. It was good because I earned some money and I didn't have so much time to think about the exams. In my free time, I met my friends, went swimming and watched a lot of TV series. I also helped my parents with some jobs around the house, like painting the fence.

But I have to say, I felt quite nervous most of the time. Sometimes I thought I had done well, and other times I remembered mistakes I had made and I felt worried. At night it was sometimes difficult to sleep. My parents told me not to worry, but it was not easy.

Finally, the results came out on a Monday morning. I checked them on the computer with my mum next to me. When I saw that I had passed with good marks, I felt so relieved and happy. I think it was the longest six weeks of my life!

answer:
The child I want to talk about is my neighbour's daughter, Leila, who was about nine years old at the time.

I've known her family for several years, because they live in the flat next to mine. Leila is a quiet, thoughtful girl who's always reading, and we sometimes chat in the lift about the books she likes.

What impressed me happened last winter. Our building has quite a few elderly residents, and one of them, an old man who lives alone on the ground floor, had a fall and broke his wrist. Leila found out about it and decided, completely on her own initiative, to organise help for him. She made a little rota on a piece of paper, knocked on every door in the building and asked people to sign up to take him meals or do his shopping on different days. When she knocked on my door, she explained the whole plan very clearly and politely, and I was so surprised that I signed up immediately.

Within a couple of days, almost every flat had volunteered. The old man told me later that he hadn't felt so cared for in years.

I was impressed for several reasons. First, she noticed a problem that most adults in the building had ignored. Second, she didn't just feel sorry for him – she actually came up with a practical solution and had the confidence to ask strangers for help. And finally, she managed to bring our whole building together. Honestly, I think many adults could learn something from her.

Describe a time when you helped a stranger.

answer:
I'd like to talk about a time I helped a tourist who was lost at a train station in my city.

It happened about a year ago, on a Sunday evening. I was waiting for a train at the central station when I noticed a young woman standing in front of the timetable board, looking completely confused. She had a huge backpack and was holding a phone that seemed to have run out of battery.

I went over and asked if she needed help. It turned out she was a student from South America who was travelling around the country on her own. She needed to get to a small town about two hours away, where she'd booked a hostel, but the last direct train had already left, and she couldn't understand the announcements. Her English was limited, and so was my Spanish, but we managed to communicate with a mixture of both languages and a lot of gestures.

I checked the connections on my phone and found that she could still get there by changing trains in another city. I walked with her to the ticket machine, helped her buy the right ticket and took her to the correct platform. I also let her use my phone to message the hostel to tell them she'd be arriving late.

Afterwards, I felt really good. She was so grateful that she gave me a hug before getting on the train. A few days later, she sent me a message to say she'd arrived safely. It reminded me how much a small act of kindness can mean to someone in a difficult situation.

The journey I'd like to describe was an overnight train trip I took across the country with my older brother about four years ago.

We were travelling from the capital to a coastal city in the far north, a distance of roughly a thousand kilometres. Flying would have been quicker, but we deliberately chose the sleeper train because we'd heard the route passed through some spectacular scenery.

We boarded at around six in the evening. For the first few hours, we sat by the window watching the city give way to farmland and then dense forest as the sun went down.

The most memorable part, though, was the dining car. It was packed with an extraordinary mix of people: a group of retired teachers on a reunion trip, a couple of soldiers going home on leave, and a family moving north for a new job. We ended up sharing a table with an elderly man who had worked on that railway line for forty years. He told us fascinating stories about blizzards that had trapped trains for days and the remote stations where his colleagues had lived.

I'd like to talk about the busiest period of my life so far, which was the final two months of my university degree.

It was in the spring of my last year. At the same time, I had to finish my final-year dissertation, which was about water pollution in local rivers, prepare for four exams, and continue working three evenings a week at a restaurant to pay my rent. I bought a large wall calendar and wrote down every deadline, and then I broke each big task into smaller steps. For example, instead of writing "finish dissertation", I'd write "complete chapter three draft" or "make graphs for results". I also started getting up at six to study for two hours before lectures, when my mind was fresh, and I turned off notifications on my phone while I was working.

I'd be lying if I said it was easy. There were days when I felt exhausted and anxious, and I definitely drank too much coffee. But once I had a clear plan, I felt much more in control. I'd like to describe a lantern festival that takes place every autumn in the town where I grew up.

It's held on the first full moon of October, along the river that runs through the old part of town. The festival has been celebrated for over two hundred years. Originally, it was a way of thanking the river for providing water for the harvest, but nowadays it's more of a community celebration.

Preparations start weeks in advance. Local schools and community groups make large paper lanterns in the shape of animals, boats and characters from local legends. On the night itself, the streets along the river are closed to traffic and filled with food stalls selling grilled corn, sweet rice cakes and hot drinks. As soon as it gets dark, there's a parade where the lanterns are carried through the streets to the sound of drums. The highlight comes at the end, when hundreds of people write wishes on small paper lanterns and float them down the river. Seeing the whole river glowing with tiny lights is absolutely magical.

I enjoy it for several reasons. Firstly, it's one of the few times of year when the whole community comes together – you see old neighbours, school friends and relatives you haven't seen for ages. Secondly, there's a wonderful mix of tradition and creativity, because every year the lantern designs are different. And finally, it brings back happy childhood memories. When I was young, I helped make lanterns with my grandfather, so every time I go, I think of him.

The person I'd like to describe is my uncle Tariq, who's without doubt the best cook in our family.

He's my mother's younger brother, and he lives about twenty minutes away from us, so I've known him all my life. He works as an electrician, so cooking isn't his job, but it's definitely his passion. Every few weeks, he invites the whole family to his house for a big Sunday lunch.

He mainly cooks dishes from the region where my mother's family comes from – slow-cooked stews with lamb and vegetables, rice flavoured with saffron and dried fruit, and freshly baked flatbreads. He's also very adventurous, though. After going on holiday, he always tries to recreate dishes he ate abroad, so we've had everything from fish curries to homemade pasta.

There are several reasons why I think he's such a good cook. First of all, he's incredibly patient. Some of his stews cook for five or six hours, and he says you can't rush good food. Secondly, he really understands how to balance flavours. He tastes everything constantly and adds a little more lemon or salt until it's just right. He never follows recipes exactly, but somehow the results are always delicious. Finally, he cooks with real generosity. He always makes far too much food, and everyone goes home with containers of leftovers.

What I admire most, though, is that he enjoys sharing his skills. Last year, he taught me how to make his famous flatbread, and although mine are nowhere near as good as his, I'm slowly improving.

answer:
The song I'd like to talk about is an old folk song from my grandmother's village. It doesn't really have an official title – everyone just calls it "The River Song".

I first heard it when I was about five or six. My grandmother used to sing it to me at bedtime whenever I stayed at her house in the summer holidays. She had a soft, slightly husky voice, and she always sang it very slowly, almost like a lullaby. At the time, I didn't really understand the words, but I loved the melody, which goes up and down like water flowing over stones.

The song tells the story of a young man who leaves his village to find work in a distant city. He promises the river that he'll return one day, and in the last verse, he comes back as an old man and finds that the river is still flowing, even though everything else has changed. It's quite a melancholy song, but there's also something comforting about it, because it suggests that some things endure.

It's special to me for a couple of reasons. Most obviously, it reminds me of my grandmother, who passed away a few years ago. Whenever I hear it, I can almost picture her sitting on the edge of my bed. But its meaning has also deepened as I've got older. When I moved abroad to study, I suddenly understood the young man in the song – the excitement of leaving, but also the longing for home. I occasionally sing it to myself when I feel homesick, and it never fails to make me feel connected to where I come from.

answer:
I'd like to talk about the first time I tried raw sea urchin, a few years ago on a business trip.

I was working for a company that sold medical equipment, and I travelled with my manager, Ms Hoffmann, to meet some clients in a coastal city in East Asia. On our last evening, the clients invited us to a small, traditional restaurant near the harbour to celebrate signing a contract. It was the kind of place with only about ten seats at a wooden counter, where the chef prepares each piece right in front of you.

Most of the meal was delicious, and I'd eaten sushi before, so I was quite relaxed. But then the chef placed something in front of me that looked like a small orange-yellow paste on top of rice, wrapped in seaweed. One of the clients explained, with a big smile, that it was sea urchin, and that it was the most special dish of the evening because it had been caught that morning.

To be honest, I was nervous. It had a very unusual texture, and I'd heard that some people find the taste too strong. But I didn't want to be rude, especially in front of our clients, so I took a deep breath and ate it in one bite. Surprisingly, it was wonderful – very creamy and soft, with a sweet taste of the sea.

I felt really proud of myself for being brave, and the clients seemed genuinely pleased that I enjoyed it. Since then, I've tried to be more open to new food when I travel, because sometimes the things that look strangest turn out to be the most delicious.

answer:
The book I'd like to recommend is a novel called The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter, which I read about two years ago. It isn't very famous, but it's one of the most memorable books I've ever read.

It's set on a small island in the North Atlantic in the early twentieth century. The main character is a girl called Elin, whose father looks after the island's lighthouse. When he becomes ill, Elin, who is only fourteen, has to take over his duties and keep the light burning every night, through storms and long, dark winters. The story follows her over about ten years as she grows up, faces loneliness and danger, and eventually has to decide whether to stay on the island or leave for the mainland.

I read it during a long, rainy holiday, when I had plenty of free time. A friend had lent it to me, and to be honest, I wasn't expecting much, because the cover looked a bit old-fashioned. But after the first chapter, I couldn't put it down.

There are several reasons I'd recommend it. First, the writing is beautiful – the author describes the sea and the weather so vividly that you can almost feel the wind. Second, Elin is a really inspiring character. She's brave and determined, but she also has doubts and makes mistakes, so she feels very real. And finally, the book raises interesting questions about duty and freedom, which made me think about my own choices.

I think it would appeal to almost anyone, whether they like adventure, history or simply a moving story.

The goal I'd like to talk about is running a half marathon, which I achieved last October.

About eighteen months before that, I was going through a difficult time. I'd just started a new job that involved sitting at a desk all day, I was sleeping badly, and I'd put on quite a lot of weight. One evening, a colleague mentioned that she was training for a half marathon, and I jokingly said I could never run that far. She replied, "Why not? Everyone starts somewhere." That conversation stayed with me, and a few days later, I decided to set myself the goal of completing a half marathon within a year and a half.

At the beginning, I could barely run for five minutes without stopping. So I downloaded a beginners' running app that combined walking and jogging, and I followed it three times a week. Gradually, I built up my distance. I also joined a local running club, which made a huge difference, because the other members encouraged me and gave me advice about shoes, stretching and nutrition. There were setbacks – I injured my knee at one point and had to rest for a month – but I didn't give up.

On the day of the race, I was incredibly nervous, especially at the start, surrounded by thousands of runners. The last three kilometres were really painful, but the crowd's cheering kept me going. When I finally crossed the finish line, after two hours and fourteen minutes, I felt an overwhelming mix of exhaustion and pride. It proved to me that big goals are achievable if you break them into small steps and stay consistent.

His influence on me was profound. Not only did I end up studying chemistry at university, but he also changed the way I think about learning. I'd like to talk about a project I worked on in my second year at university, when four of us designed a mobile app to help students find quiet places to study on campus.

It was part of a module on software design, and the lecturer put us into random groups, so I was working with three people I didn't really know: a quiet but very talented programmer called Ji-woo, a design student called Marco, and Aisha, who was brilliant at organisation.

I'd like to talk about the first time I went kayaking, which was during a summer holiday two years ago.

I was staying with some friends at a lakeside campsite in the mountains. The lake was famous for its clear turquoise water, and there was a small centre where you could rent kayaks and take lessons. My friend Kenji, who'd been kayaking several times before, persuaded me to try it, even though I'm not a very confident swimmer.

But after a while, I found a rhythm, and I started to relax and enjoy it. The lake was completely calm, and the only sounds were the paddles in the water and birds in the trees. At one point, we stopped in the middle of the lake and just floated, looking up at the mountains. It was one of the most peaceful moments I've ever experienced.

By the end of the day, my arms were aching, but I felt really proud that I'd overcome my nerves. I've been kayaking three more times since then.

I'd like to talk about a disagreement I had with my close friend Nadia about two years ago, when we were planning a trip together.

We'd been saving up for months to travel together after graduating, and we'd agreed on a budget and a three-week timeframe. The problem arose when we started planning the details. Nadia wanted to visit as many cities as possible – she'd drawn up an itinerary that included eight different places in three weeks. I, on the other hand, wanted to stay in two or three places and really get to know them.

Looking back, our different opinions reflected our personalities. Nadia is incredibly energetic and hates the idea of missing out on anything, whereas I find constant travelling exhausting and prefer a slower pace. There was also a financial aspect: I'd calculated that moving around so much would mean spending a large part of our budget on transport.

For a few days, things got quite tense. We exchanged some rather sharp messages. Eventually, we agreed to meet in person rather than arguing by text, which made a huge difference. We each explained what we really wanted from the trip, and we realised that we both wanted the same basic thing – to have a memorable time together. In the end, we compromised on five places, and we agreed that on a couple of days, we'd each do our own thing.

Afterwards, I felt relieved and, to be honest, slightly embarrassed that we'd let such a small issue become so heated. But the trip was fantastic, and I think the experience strengthened our friendship, because we learned how to listen to each other.

I'd like to talk about the final of a regional basketball tournament that I watched live about three years ago.

The rule I'd like to talk about was a ban on mobile phones at my secondary school, which was introduced when I was about fifteen.

The rule was quite strict. Students had to hand in their phones at the school office when they arrived in the morning and could only collect them at the end of the day. Anyone caught with a phone during school hours had it confiscated for a week, and their parents were called in.

I understood the reasoning behind it. The school was concerned that students were distracted in lessons and that phones were being used for cyberbullying, which were legitimate worries. However, I disagreed with the way it was implemented, for several reasons. Firstly, it was a blanket ban that didn't distinguish between misuse and genuinely useful purposes – for example, some students relied on their phones to coordinate travel home, or had parents who were ill and needed to reach them. Secondly, I felt it was a missed opportunity. Rather than teaching us how to use technology responsibly, which is a skill we'd need for life, the school simply removed the problem. And thirdly, it was introduced without any consultation with students, which made it feel imposed rather than agreed.

Interestingly, the rule was eventually modified, partly because of a campaign led by the student council, which I was a member of. We collected feedback, presented a proposal to the head teacher, and after a term of discussions, the school agreed to a compromise: phones stayed in lockers during lessons, but students could use them at lunchtime. I learned a lot from that experience about how to challenge a decision constructively, using evidence rather than simply complaining.

A place I'd really love to visit one day is Iceland, the island in the North Atlantic.

I first became interested in it about five years ago, when I watched a documentary about volcanoes. A large part of it was filmed there, and I was amazed by the landscapes – black sand beaches, huge glaciers, waterfalls and steaming hot springs, all within a relatively small area. Since then, I've read quite a few travel blogs about it, and a friend of mine went there last year and showed me hundreds of photos, which made me even more determined to go.

I know you need to go in winter and be quite lucky with the weather, but seeing the sky lit up with green and purple light must be unforgettable. I'd also like to go on a guided walk on a glacier, wearing special boots with spikes, and visit one of the natural hot springs, where you can bathe outside even when it's freezing. And I'd like to rent a car and drive around the island, stopping in small fishing villages along the way.

There are a few reasons I want to go there. I've always been fascinated by nature and geology, and Iceland seems like a place where you can actually see the forces that shape the Earth – there are active volcanoes and geysers. It's also very different from my home country, which is hot and crowded, so I think I'd find the space and silence really refreshing. I'm hoping to save enough money to go within the next two or three years.

The library itself is in a grand nineteenth-century building in the city centre, but most visitors only use the busy ground floor, where you can borrow books and use the computers. Most of the time I study or read, but sometimes I just sit by the window and watch the rain falling on the rooftops. I like going there for several reasons. First, it's one of the few places where I can concentrate completely. Being surrounded by old books makes me feel connected to all the people who studied there before me. And finally, it's a good place to escape from the noise of the city. I'd like to describe a tradition in my family that we call "Sunday soup". It's simple, but it means a lot to all of us.

As far as I know, it started with my great-grandmother about seventy years ago. She was a widow with five children and not much money, and every Sunday she would make a huge pot of soup with whatever vegetables were cheap that week. Her children, and later their families, would come to her house to share it. When she died, my grandmother continued the tradition, and now my mother has taken over.

What we do is quite straightforward. Every Sunday at around one o'clock, whoever is free comes to my parents' house. There are usually between eight and fifteen people – my parents, my grandparents, my aunts and uncles, my cousins and their children. My mother makes the soup, but everyone brings something to share, like bread, salad or a dessert. We eat together around a long table, and afterwards the adults drink coffee and talk while the children play in the garden. There's no pressure to come every week, but most of us come at least twice a month.

This tradition is important to me for several reasons. Most importantly, it keeps our family close. We all have busy lives and live in different parts of the city, so without Sunday soup, I think we'd only see each other at weddings and funerals. I'd like to talk about a time I got lost while hiking in a national park about three years ago.

I was on holiday with two friends, and we decided to do a day hike along a trail that was described in our guidebook as "moderate", about fifteen kilometres long. The weather forecast was good, so we set off early in the morning with water, sandwiches and a paper map, which we thought would be enough.

For the first few hours, everything went smoothly. The trail was clearly marked with red paint on trees and rocks. But around midday, we came to a point where the path split into two, and the marking wasn't very clear. We chose the left path, which seemed wider, but after about an hour, we realised we hadn't seen any red marks for a long time. To make things worse, clouds came in, so we couldn't see the mountains we'd been using as landmarks, and there was no phone signal.

At first, we argued a bit about what to do, but eventually we agreed that the safest option was to go back the way we'd come. It took us almost two hours to return to the point where the path divided, and from there we followed the correct trail. We finally got back to the car park just as it was getting dark, completely exhausted.

Honestly, for a while I felt quite scared, especially when the clouds came in and I started to imagine spending the night outside. But afterwards, I felt relieved and also a bit embarrassed that we'd been so unprepared. I learned an important lesson: always download offline maps and tell someone where you're going.

answer:
The habit I'd really like to change is checking my phone first thing in the morning and last thing at night.

I think it started about five years ago, when I got my first smartphone and started using it as an alarm clock. Since my phone was right next to my bed, it became natural to pick it up as soon as I turned the alarm off. At first, I'd just look at the time and the weather, but gradually it turned into scrolling through social media, reading the news and replying to messages, often for twenty or thirty minutes before I even got out of bed. The same thing happens at night – I tell myself I'll just check one thing, and before I know it, it's an hour later.

This habit affects me in several ways. In the mornings, I often end up rushing because I've wasted time, and I sometimes start the day feeling anxious, especially if I've read bad news or a stressful work email. At night, it definitely affects my sleep, because I often lie awake thinking about things I've just seen online. As a result, I feel tired during the day.

I'd like to change it because I want to start and end my days more calmly. I've already taken a few steps. I've bought an old-fashioned alarm clock, and I'm trying to leave my phone charging in the kitchen overnight. Instead, I've started reading a book before bed. It's not easy, and I still slip back into the habit sometimes, but I've noticed that on the days I manage it, I feel much more relaxed and focused.

answer:
I'd like to describe what happened when my laptop crashed in the middle of a presentation I was giving to a potential client, about a year ago.

At the time, I was working for a small design agency, and we'd been invited to pitch for a contract with a large hotel chain. It was a big deal for us – the contract would have been worth more than our total income for the previous six months. I'd spent weeks preparing the presentation, which included videos, animations and examples of our previous work.

The meeting took place in the client's head office, in a conference room with a huge screen. About ten minutes into the presentation, just as I was about to show our main concept, the screen suddenly went black. My laptop had frozen completely, and when I restarted it, a message appeared saying it needed to install an update, which would take at least twenty minutes.

For a few seconds, I genuinely panicked. But then I remembered that I'd brought printed copies of the key slides as a backup, which my manager had always insisted on. I apologised, handed them out and continued the presentation using the printouts and a whiteboard, sketching some of the ideas by hand. In a way, it made the meeting more interactive, because the clients started asking questions and adding their own suggestions.

Looking back, I felt a mixture of embarrassment and pride. It was mortifying at the moment it happened, but I was proud that I'd stayed calm and improvised. And, as it turned out, we won the contract. Since then, I always disable automatic updates before an important presentation.

I'd like to talk about my neighbour Mr Kim, who lives in the house next to my parents' house.

Mr Kim is about seventy years old. He used to be a mathematics teacher at a high school, but he retired about ten years ago. He lives with his wife, and they have two sons who live in other cities. He is quite short and has white hair, and he almost always wears a hat when he is outside.

I have known him for about fifteen years, since my family moved into our house when I was eight. At first, I was a little scared of him, because he looked very serious. But one day, my football went over the fence into his garden, and when I went to get it, he gave it back to me with a big smile and some fruit from his tree. After that, we became friends.

When I was at school, Mr Kim often helped me with my maths homework. He was very patient and explained things in a very clear way, much better than my teachers! Now, when I visit my parents, I usually go to see him too. We sit in his garden and talk about many things, like the news, sport and my job. Sometimes I help him with his computer or his phone, because he finds technology difficult.

I like him because he is kind, funny and very wise. He always gives me good advice, and he is interested in my life. He is like a grandfather to me, and I think our street is a better place because of him.

I'd like to talk about a wooden bookshelf that I made by hand last year.

I'd just moved into a new flat, and I needed somewhere to keep my books, but all the bookshelves I liked in shops were either too expensive or the wrong size for the space next to my desk. My uncle is a keen amateur carpenter, and when I mentioned this to him, he suggested that I make one myself in his workshop, with his help.

First, I measured the space carefully and drew a simple design on paper – a shelf about one metre high, with three levels. Then my uncle took me to a timber yard, where we chose some pine wood. Back in his workshop, he showed me how to cut the pieces to the right length using a saw, and how to sand the edges until they were smooth. The hardest part was making the joints, because they had to be very precise, otherwise the shelf would wobble. Finally, I glued and screwed everything together and applied two coats of natural oil to protect the wood.

Altogether, it took about four weekends, working for a few hours each time. It probably would have been quicker and cheaper to buy one, but that wasn't really the point.

I felt incredibly satisfied when it was finished. It isn't perfect – if you look closely, one of the shelves is very slightly uneven – but I love it because I made it myself. Every time I look at it, I remember the time I spent with my uncle, and it's inspired me to try more woodwork projects.
